entries.name: Antarctic hair grass
entries.leaves: narrow flat blades, evergreen
entries.flowers: small green panicle, wind-pollinated, in summer
entries.voxel_shape: small green tussock tuft of narrow blades hugging bare rock and peat
entries.notes: One of only two native flowering plants in Antarctica. Grows photosynthesising at near-freezing temperatures; expanding fast with warming — a living thermometer on the peninsula.

entries.name: Antarctic pearlwort
entries.leaves: tiny spoon-shaped leaves in dense moss-like cushions
entries.voxel_shape: dense moss-like cushion, one or two blocks of yellow flecked green in season
entries.notes: The other native Antarctic flowering plant. Its spread into new ice-free ground is one of the clearest botanical signals of Antarctic warming.

entries.name: Red snow alga
entries.voxel_shape: not a model — tints snow pink to blood-red, including a faint sweet smell
entries.notes: Microscopic cells (20–30 micrometres) blooming to 25 cm depth give snow its red hue; now mostly placed in genus Sanguina (S. nivaloides, S. aurantia for orange). A teaspoon of melted red snow holds a million or more cells.

entries.name: Dark ice alga
entries.voxel_shape: not a model — darkens bare ice in grey-violet streaks
uses: drives ice-sheet surface darkening and melt (bioalbedo)
entries.notes: Heavily pigmented alga of the bare-ice zone; blooms can reach 100,000 cells/ml. The darkening measurably speeds Greenland Ice Sheet melt and has been detected on Antarctic ice too.

entries.name: Map lichen
entries.voxel_shape: flat lime-green crust on exposed rock, bordered by black fungal line, like a drawn map
uses: lichenometry — dating ice retreat and moraines
entries.notes: Grows about 16 mm in diameter per century in the maritime Antarctic; one East Baffin Island specimen is estimated at 9,500 years, and Brooks Range estimates run to 10,000–11,500. It survived 10 days exposed in space.

entries.name: Elegant sunburst lichen
entries.voxel_shape: small orange to yellow rosette crust on bird-influenced rock
entries.notes: Survived 18 months exposed on the ISS (EXPOSE-E) and simulated Mars conditions; classic orange coating on coastal Antarctic and Arctic rock. Loved by lichens-for-dating studies less than Rhizocarpon, but the astrobiology icon.

entries.name: Antarctic grimmia
entries.leaves: small pointed leaves, brown to dark green or reddish
entries.voxel_shape: dense cushion or continuous moss bed on rock and soil
entries.notes: One of the most widespread and abundant mosses in Antarctica, endemic to the continent; forms continuous beds across the Peninsula, South Shetlands and parts of east Antarctica.

entries.name: Purple roof moss
entries.leaves: tiny lance-shaped leaves, often reddish-awned, forming dense tufts
entries.fruit: red-brown twisted capsule on a long seta
entries.voxel_shape: small reddish-green cushion tuft with a red-capped bristle
entries.notes: Arguably the most cosmopolitan moss on Earth; recorded at the southernmost Antarctic sites (Botany Bay, Ross Sea). One of the first plants onto fresh deglaciated ground and burned soil.

entries.name: Arctic sea lettuce
entries.voxel_shape: dark green lettuce-like rosettes and turfs on splash-zone rock near ice
entries.notes: Forms vast dark green turfs on splash-zone and bird-fertilised coastal rock in ice-locked seas. In the Dry Valleys it survives on meltwater and ground frost rather than liquid seas.

entries.name: Fishbone beard lichen
entries.voxel_shape: pale grey-green beard strands hanging from cliff and boulder edges
entries.notes: A fruticose pendant lichen common on coastal Antarctic rock and tundra boulders; like all Usnea, sensitive to air pollution, so a living clean-air badge in a world of ice.

entries.name: Antarctic moss fungus
entries.voxel_shape: one tiny brown cap rising from a moss carpet
entries.notes: Originally described as Omphalina antarctica; the first native macromycete described from Antarctica. Grows on bryophyte mats in maritime Antarctica — a mushroom in the coldest flowering-plant-free land.

entries.name: Polar willow
entries.leaves: small rounded leaves in dense prostrate mats, evergreen
entries.voxel_shape: prostrate creeping mat of tiny leaves on nunatak rock
entries.notes: One of the world's smallest willows; survives on nunataks (rock islands in the ice) and in glacier-retreat forefields in Svalbard and Greenland. A real shrub living inside the ice-sheet biome's edges.

entries.name: Purple saxifrage
entries.leaves: tiny opposite scale-like leaves in four ranks, evergreen, lime-encrusted
entries.flowers: solitary purple-pink, first to bloom after snowmelt
entries.voxel_shape: flat cushion of dark evergreen with purple stars
entries.notes: The northernmost flowering plant on Earth (Kaffeklubben Island, 83°N, north of Greenland) and the highest in the Alps (4,505 m). Nunataks and ice-sheet margins in Greenland are classic habitat.

entries.name: Arctic poppy
entries.leaves: grey-hairy pinnate leaves in a basal rosette
entries.flowers: yellow to white, four petals, heliotrope (faces the sun)
entries.voxel_shape: single sun-tracking cup of yellow on a hairy grey stem
uses: landmark flower on bare nunatak rock
entries.notes: Grows a few inches high on northern Greenland's icy coasts and nunataks; heliotropic like a sunflower, funnelling heat to its dark centre for pollinating insects. Poppy pollen in GISP2 ice cores shows central Greenland was once tundra.

entries.name: Mountain avens
entries.leaves: small evergreen oak-shaped leaves, white-felted beneath
entries.flowers: eight white petals (rarely 5–16), rose family, sun-tracking
entries.voxel_shape: low evergreen mat with white saucer flowers and silky seed heads
entries.notes: The Younger Dryas cold snap is named for it — its pollen dominates ice-core samples from that era. Clonal genets age to 500+ years; it grew near the Greenland ice margin and Iceland is its national flower.

entries.name: Dwarf willow
entries.leaves: tiny rounded leaves pressed flat, evergreen
entries.voxel_shape: flat creeping mat plant, top of exposed ice-free ledges
entries.notes: The world's smallest willow; mats of it carpet the margins of ice-free ledges and snowbeds in the far north and on high mountains, right up to ice caps.

entries.name: Arctic willow
entries.leaves: rounded leaves on hairy creeping stems
entries.voxel_shape: low tangled creeping shrub hugging nunatak gravel
uses: reindeer forage on High Arctic coasts
entries.notes: The classic willow of Thule, north Greenland; creeping and ancient — some genets near Peary Land are centuries old on nunataks between ice caps.

entries.name: Alpine haircap moss
entries.leaves: stiff narrow leaves with a toothed tip, blue-green
entries.fruit: four-angled capsule like a tiny hairy drum
entries.voxel_shape: upright star-pointed turfs, the tallest moss in polar patches
entries.notes: Bipolar — found in moss communities on both the Antarctic Peninsula and High Arctic nunataks; one of the tallest mosses of the ice-edge communities.

entries.name: Sickle-leaved hook moss
entries.leaves: strongly hooked leaves curving one way, glossy green
entries.voxel_shape: glossy green sickle-leaf carpets in sheltered polar hollows
entries.notes: A dominant moss of Arctic and Antarctic moist hollows; hooked leaves all curve the same way, an easy ID for explorers and modders alike.

entries.name: Nodding thread moss
entries.leaves: small keeled leaves clustered at stem tips
entries.voxel_shape: thread-thin green stems with nodding capsules
entries.notes: Nearly universal in polar moss beds; one of the commonest mosses on both ice continents, often under snow right into the growing season.

entries.name: Marsh bryum
entries.leaves: broad leaves with a red stem base, forming tufts
entries.voxel_shape: red-based moss tufts in melt-water seeps
entries.notes: The moss of polar mires and meltwater seeps; fed by summer melt channels across ice-free ground at both poles.

entries.name: Black rock moss
entries.leaves: tiny black-green leaves, splitting capsule (no lid)
entries.fruit: capsule splitting lengthwise into four teeth
entries.voxel_shape: black cushion dots on bare granite rock
entries.notes: An ancient lineage — Andreaea splits its spore capsule into four slits instead of popping a lid. Black rock moss is a granite specialist at both poles.

entries.name: Silvergreen bryum
entries.leaves: silvery-white pointed leaves when dry
entries.voxel_shape: silvery cushion dotting cracks in polar rock
uses: tiny pioneer on disturbed polar and urban ground
entries.notes: The world's most cosmopolitan moss — pavement, rooftops, Antarctic research stations. If an ice-free patch is disturbed by boots or drills, this is among the first back.

entries.name: Crispate dicranoweisia
entries.leaves: curled (crispate) leaves when dry, spreading when wet
entries.voxel_shape: crisp curled tufts that uncurl after meltwater
entries.notes: Bipolar polar-alpine moss; desiccation-tolerant curled leaves make it a champion of drought-prone nunatak ledges.

entries.name: Bryoerythrophyllum recurvirostrum
entries.leaves: reddish-brown ovate leaves in loose tufts
entries.voxel_shape: red-brown tuft on wind-blasted polar soil
entries.notes: Recorded at Botany Bay, Ross Sea — the southernmost moss record for continental Antarctica; a marker of the harshest dry continental interior.

entries.name: Antarctic liverwort
entries.leaves: tiny two-lobed leaves, often reddish, flat rosettes
entries.voxel_shape: microscopic red-green rosette inside moss carpets
entries.notes: The commonest liverwort in Antarctica and the only hepatic known above 70°S; hides inside moss cushions in well-drained maritime sites.

entries.name: Antarctic rock tripe
entries.voxel_shape: black paper-thin discs stuck to wind-scoured boulders
uses: indicator of extreme cold and dryness
entries.notes: A foliose rock-tripe lichen of the Dry Valleys and continental margins; anhydrobiotic — survives decades desiccated, then revives in minutes of melt.

entries.name: Decussate rock tripe
entries.voxel_shape: overlapping grey-black rosette plates on coastal rock
entries.notes: Common on bird-fertilised coastal rocks around the Antarctic Peninsula; fat thalli near penguin rookeries betray the guano trail.

entries.name: Common sulphur lichen
entries.voxel_shape: golden-yellow crust splash on sunlit rock
uses: bright accent for barren ice-free ledges
entries.notes: Bipolar yellow crust of bird-influenced rock; partner in crime to X. elegans along Antarctic and Arctic coasts.

entries.name: Alpine tobacco lichen
entries.voxel_shape: grey-white branching coral tufts on glacial grit
uses: pioneer on glacial till and moraine
entries.notes: Grey coral-like fruticose lichen of fresh glacial till; its photosymbiont partnership helps build soil on raw ground where nothing else grows.

entries.name: Grey hoary rosette lichen
entries.voxel_shape: pale grey hoary star rosettes on coastal Antarctic rock
entries.notes: One of the commonest foliose lichens in both polar regions; pale hoary rosettes star the coastal rocks from Greenland to the Antarctic Peninsula.

entries.name: Black witches' hair
entries.voxel_shape: wind-tortured black horsehair tufts on exposed ice-edge rock
entries.notes: A wind-blast specialist: black wiry cushions plastered flat on nunatak summits and dry Antarctic valleys, where desiccation and cold rule together.

entries.name: Turgidosculum complicatulum
entries.voxel_shape: near-invisible dark crust on the driest Antarctic soil
entries.notes: Southernmost record for the genus, from Botany Bay, Ross Sea; an expert-level lichen of the Antarctic Dry Valleys, where the ground may see no liquid water for years.

entries.name: Abbreviated bluegrass
entries.leaves: short blue-grey blades in tight tufts
entries.voxel_shape: tiny blue-grey tuft on polar barrens
entries.notes: High Arctic bluegrass of the coldest, driest nunatak barrens — the sort of grass that survives where Greenland's ice creeps downhill into its habitat.

entries.name: Milky whitlowgrass
entries.leaves: small hairy leaves in a basal rosette
entries.flowers: small white cross-shaped flowers, mustard family
entries.voxel_shape: minute white-starred rosette on nunatak gravel
entries.notes: High Arctic whitlowgrass like a pinpoint of white on black nunatak rock; one of the few flowering plants pushing into Greenland's ice-free interior.
